title: Bechamel
subtitle: Classic white sauce made with butter, flour, and milk
excerpt: The fundamental white sauce of French and Italian cooking: butter and flour cooked together, then whisked with warm milk until thick, silky, and smooth. The base for lasagne, cauliflower cheese, and croquettes.

recipe.sourceNotes: Bechamel (or besciamella in Italian) is one of the five classic French mother sauces codified by Auguste Escoffier in the late nineteenth century. The name is associated with Louis de Bechameil, the Marquis de Nointel and steward to Louis XIV, though the sauce itself predates him and was likely brought to France by Italian cooks accompanying Catherine de Medici in the sixteenth century. The sauce is made from a roux (equal weights of butter and flour cooked together) to which warm or hot milk is added. The key principles are: the roux must be cooked for at least 2 minutes to eliminate the raw flour taste; the milk should be warm or hot rather than cold (cold milk produces lumps); and the sauce must be stirred constantly to prevent burning on the base. Bechamel is the basis for Mornay sauce (with cheese), soubise (with onion), and is the white sauce used in pasta al forno dishes such as lasagne.

content.text: The most common mistake with bechamel is adding cold milk to a hot roux, which causes lumps. Warm the milk gently in a separate saucepan before adding. If the sauce does develop lumps, pass it through a sieve or blend it briefly with a stick blender: this rescues even a badly lumpy sauce. The sauce should be cooked over a medium heat after all the milk is in, stirring constantly, until it is thick enough to coat the back of a spoon and leaves a channel when a finger is drawn across it.

Warm the milk gently in a saucepan with the bay leaf until steaming but not boiling. Melt the butter in a separate heavy saucepan over medium heat. Add the flour and stir constantly with a wooden spoon for 2 minutes: the roux should smell biscuity but not colour.

Remove the bay leaf. Add the warm milk to the roux a ladleful at a time, whisking vigorously after each addition to incorporate without lumps. When all the milk is in, switch to a wooden spoon and stir constantly over medium heat for 8 to 10 minutes until the sauce is thick and smooth.
Season with salt, pepper, and freshly grated nutmeg. Taste: the sauce should have no floury taste. Use immediately, or press a sheet of cling film directly onto the surface to prevent a skin forming.
